# How Machines "See" Images 👁️ {background-color="#2d4563"}

## Think about this 🤔
### A challenge for you

:::{style="margin-top: 40px; font-size: 28px;"}

> **Imagine you need to describe an image to a computer that only understands numbers.**
>
> How would you do it?

:::{.fragment}
**Discuss with your neighbour for 1 minute!** ⏱️

- What information would you include?
- How would you represent colours? Shapes? Objects?
- What makes this problem hard?
:::

:::{.fragment}
:::{style="margin-top: 30px;"}
**The key insight**: Just like text needs to become numbers (tokens → embeddings), [images need to become numbers too]{.alert}!
:::
:::
:::

## What computers actually see
### Images as grids of numbers

:::{style="margin-top: 30px; font-size: 24px;"}
:::{.columns}
:::{.column width=55%}
- A digital image is just a [grid of pixels]{.alert}
- Each pixel has numerical values:
  - **Grayscale**: One number (0–255)
  - **Colour (RGB)**: Three numbers (Red, Green, Blue)
- A 224×224 colour image = [150,528 numbers!]{.alert}
  - $224 \times 224 \times 3 = 150,528$
- The challenge: How do we find [meaningful patterns]{.alert} in all these numbers?
- Raw pixels don't tell us "this is a cat" — we need [smarter processing]{.alert}
:::

:::{.column width=45%}
:::{style="text-align: center;"}
[![A pixel grid with RGB values](figures/pixel-grid.png){width="100%"}](#){data-modal-type="image" data-modal-url="figures/pixel-grid.png"}

:::{style="font-size: 18px; margin-top: 10px;"}
Each pixel: three values from 0 (black) to 255 (brightest)
:::
:::
:::
:::
:::

## The convolution operation
### A "sliding magnifying glass"

:::{style="margin-top: 30px; font-size: 24px;"}
:::{.columns}
:::{.column width=55%}
- [Convolution]{.alert}: A small filter "slides" across the image
- At each position, it performs element-wise multiplication and sums the result
- Different filters detect different features:
  - Vertical edges, horizontal edges
  - Corners, textures, gradients
- The filter [learns what to look for]{.alert} during training!
- Output: A [feature map]{.alert} showing where that feature appears

:::{style="margin-top: 20px;"}
**Analogy**: Like using a stencil to find specific patterns 🔍
:::
:::

:::{.column width=45%}
:::{style="text-align: center;"}
[![Convolution: filter sliding over image](figures/convolution-animation.gif){width="100%"}](#){data-modal-type="image" data-modal-url="figures/convolution-animation.gif"}

Source: [vdumoulin/conv_arithmetic](https://github.com/vdumoulin/conv_arithmetic)
:::
:::
:::
:::

## Feature hierarchies
### From edges to objects

:::{style="margin-top: 30px; font-size: 24px;"}
:::{.columns}
:::{.column width=50%}
- CNNs stack [multiple convolutional layers]{.alert}
- Each layer builds on the previous one:
  - **Layer 1**: Simple edges and colours
  - **Layer 2**: Textures and corners
  - **Layer 3**: Parts (eyes, wheels, leaves)
  - **Layer 4+**: Whole objects and scenes
- This is called a [feature hierarchy]{.alert}
- The network learns to [compose simple features into complex concepts]{.alert}
- Similar to how our visual cortex works!
:::

:::{.column width=50%}
:::{style="text-align: center;"}
[![Feature hierarchy: edges → textures → parts → objects](figures/feature-hierarchy.png){width="100%"}](#){data-modal-type="image" data-modal-url="figures/feature-hierarchy.png"}

Source: [Zeiler & Fergus (2014)](https://arxiv.org/abs/1311.2901)
:::
:::
:::
:::

## Pooling: Making it robust
### Downsampling for efficiency

:::{style="margin-top: 30px; font-size: 24px;"}
:::{.columns}
:::{.column width=55%}
- [Pooling]{.alert} reduces the spatial dimensions
- Most common: [Max pooling]{.alert}
  - Take the maximum value in each small region
  - E.g., 2×2 pooling: 224×224 → 112×112
- Benefits:
  - [Reduces computation]{.alert} (fewer numbers to process)
  - [Translation invariance]{.alert}: A cat is still a cat if shifted slightly
  - Forces the network to focus on [what's there, not exactly where]{.alert}
- Typical CNN: Alternates convolution and pooling layers
:::

:::{.column width=45%}
:::{style="text-align: center;"}
[![Max pooling takes the largest value in each region](figures/pooling-diagram.png){width="100%"}](#){data-modal-type="image" data-modal-url="figures/pooling-diagram.png"}

:::{style="font-size: 18px; margin-top: 10px;"}
2×2 max pooling: Keep only the maximum value
:::
:::
:::
:::
:::

## The full CNN architecture
### Putting it all together

:::{style="margin-top: 30px; font-size: 22px;"}
:::{.columns}
:::{.column width=100%}
:::{style="text-align: center;"}
[![CNN architecture: Input → Conv → Pool → Conv → Pool → Flatten → Dense → Output](figures/cnn-architecture.png){width="95%"}](#){data-modal-type="image" data-modal-url="figures/cnn-architecture.png"}
:::

:::{style="margin-top: 20px;"}
1. **Input**: Raw image (e.g., 224×224×3)
2. **Convolutional layers**: Extract features (edges → textures → objects)
3. **Pooling layers**: Reduce dimensions, add robustness
4. **Flatten**: Convert 2D feature maps to 1D vector
5. **Fully connected layers**: Combine features for final decision
6. **Output**: Class probabilities (e.g., 90% cat, 8% dog, 2% bird)
:::
:::
:::
:::

## Vision Transformers (ViT)
### "An Image is Worth 16×16 Words"

:::{style="margin-top: 30px; font-size: 24px;"}
:::{.columns}
:::{.column width=55%}
- In 2020, researchers asked: [Can we use Transformers for images?]{.alert}
- Key idea: Treat image patches like tokens!
- The process:
  1. **Divide** image into fixed-size patches (e.g., 16×16 pixels)
  2. **Flatten** each patch into a vector
  3. **Add positional embeddings** (so model knows patch locations)
  4. **Process through Transformer** (same attention mechanism as LLMs!)
- Why it matters: [Same architecture for text AND images]{.alert}
- Foundation for multimodal models like GPT-4V and Gemini
:::

:::{.column width=45%}
:::{style="text-align: center;"}
[![Vision Transformer architecture](figures/vit-architecture.png){width="100%"}](#){data-modal-type="image" data-modal-url="figures/vit-architecture.png"}

Source: [Dosovitskiy et al. (2020)](https://arxiv.org/abs/2010.11929)
:::
:::
:::
:::

## ViT: The maths (simplified!)
### Patches as tokens

:::{style="margin-top: 30px; font-size: 24px;"}
:::{.columns}
:::{.column width=55%}
- For a 224×224 image with 16×16 patches:

$$N_{\text{patches}} = \frac{224 \times 224}{16 \times 16} = \frac{50,176}{256} = 196 \text{ patches}$$

- Each patch becomes a vector of 768 dimensions
- Just like tokens in an LLM!
- The Transformer then applies [self-attention]{.alert} across all patches
- Patches can "look at" other patches to understand context
- Result: The model learns [which parts of the image matter for the task]{.alert}
:::

:::{.column width=45%}
:::{style="text-align: center;"}
[![Image split into patches, then processed like text tokens](figures/vit-patches.png){width="100%"}](#){data-modal-type="image" data-modal-url="figures/vit-patches.png"}

:::{style="font-size: 18px; margin-top: 10px;"}
196 patches = 196 "visual tokens" for the Transformer
:::
:::
:::
:::
:::

# Computer Vision Tasks 🎯 {background-color="#2d4563"}

## Three fundamental tasks
### What can computers do with images?

:::{style="margin-top: 30px; font-size: 22px;"}
:::{.columns}
:::{.column width=100%}
:::{style="text-align: center;"}
[![Classification vs Detection vs Segmentation](figures/vision-tasks-comparison.png){width="90%"}](#){data-modal-type="image" data-modal-url="figures/vision-tasks-comparison.png"}
:::

| Task | Question | Output | Example |
|------|----------|--------|---------|
| [Classification]{.alert} | "What is this?" | Single label | "This is a cat" |
| [Detection]{.alert} | "What and where?" | Bounding boxes + labels | "Cat at (x,y), dog at (x,y)" |
| [Segmentation]{.alert} | "Which pixels belong to what?" | Pixel-level masks | Every pixel labelled |

:::
:::
:::

## Object detection in action
### YOLO: You Only Look Once

:::{style="margin-top: 30px; font-size: 24px;"}
:::{.columns}
:::{.column width=55%}
- [Object detection]{.alert}: Find AND localise multiple objects
- [YOLO]{.alert} (2016): Real-time detection
  - Processes entire image in one pass
  - Outputs bounding boxes + class probabilities
  - Fast enough for video (30+ FPS)
- Applications:
  - [Self-driving cars]{.alert}: Detect pedestrians, vehicles, signs
  - [Security]{.alert}: Track people, detect intrusions
  - [Retail]{.alert}: Inventory management, checkout-free stores
  - [Sports]{.alert}: Player tracking, ball detection
:::

:::{.column width=45%}
:::{style="text-align: center;"}
[![YOLO detecting objects in a street scene](figures/yolo-detection.png){width="100%"}](#){data-modal-type="image" data-modal-url="figures/yolo-detection.png"}

Source: [Ultralytics YOLO](https://docs.ultralytics.com/)
:::
:::
:::
:::

## CLIP: Connecting images and text
### The bridge to multimodal AI

:::{style="margin-top: 30px; font-size: 24px;"}
:::{.columns}
:::{.column width=55%}
- [CLIP]{.alert} (Contrastive Language-Image Pre-training) by OpenAI
- Trained on [400 million image-text pairs]{.alert} from the internet
- Key innovation: [Shared embedding space]{.alert} for images AND text
- How it works:
  - Image encoder → image embedding
  - Text encoder → text embedding
  - Train so matching pairs are [close together]{.alert}
- Result: Can match images to text descriptions [without task-specific training]{.alert}
- Foundation for DALL-E, Stable Diffusion, and multimodal LLMs!
:::

:::{.column width=45%}
:::{style="text-align: center;"}
[![CLIP learns to match images with their text descriptions](figures/clip-training.png){width="100%"}](#){data-modal-type="image" data-modal-url="figures/clip-training.png"}

Source: [OpenAI CLIP](https://openai.com/research/clip)
:::
:::
:::
:::

# How Machines "Hear" Audio 🎵 {background-color="#2d4563"}

## Discussion: The audio challenge 🤔
### How would YOU do it?

:::{style="margin-top: 40px; font-size: 28px;"}

> **Sound is invisible vibrations in the air.**
>
> How would you convert sound into something a computer can process?

:::{.fragment}
**Take 30 seconds to think, then share with your neighbour!** ⏱️

- What properties of sound could be measured?
- How is this similar to or different from images?
:::

:::{.fragment}
:::{style="margin-top: 30px;"}
**Key insight**: We can [visualise sound]{.alert}—and then process it like an image! 🖼️
:::
:::
:::

## Waveforms vs spectrograms
### Two ways to "see" sound

:::{style="margin-top: 30px; font-size: 24px;"}
:::{.columns}
:::{.column width=50%}
**Waveform:**

- Raw representation of sound
- X-axis: Time
- Y-axis: Amplitude (loudness)
- Very detailed but [hard to interpret]{.alert}
- CD audio: 44,100 samples per second!

:::{style="text-align: center; margin-top: 20px;"}
[![Waveform representation](figures/waveform.png){width="90%"}](#){data-modal-type="image" data-modal-url="figures/waveform.png"}
:::
:::

:::{.column width=50%}
**Spectrogram:**

- Visual representation with [three dimensions]{.alert}:
  - X-axis: Time
  - Y-axis: Frequency (pitch)
  - Colour: Intensity (loudness)
- Much easier for ML models!
- [Can be processed like an image]{.alert} 🎯

:::{style="text-align: center; margin-top: 20px;"}
[![Spectrogram representation](figures/spectrogram.png){width="90%"}](#){data-modal-type="image" data-modal-url="figures/spectrogram.png"}
:::
:::
:::
:::

## The mel scale
### Matching human hearing

:::{style="margin-top: 30px; font-size: 24px;"}
:::{.columns}
:::{.column width=55%}
- Humans don't hear all frequencies equally
- We're [more sensitive to lower frequencies]{.alert}
- The [mel scale]{.alert} adjusts for this:
  - More resolution for low frequencies (speech fundamentals)
  - Less resolution for high frequencies
- [Mel spectrogram]{.alert}: Spectrogram mapped to mel scale
- This is the [standard input]{.alert} for most audio ML models!
- Named after "melody"—designed for music and speech perception
:::

:::{.column width=45%}
:::{style="text-align: center;"}
[![Mel spectrogram of human speech](figures/mel-spectrogram.png){width="100%"}](#){data-modal-type="image" data-modal-url="figures/mel-spectrogram.png"}

:::{style="font-size: 18px; margin-top: 10px;"}
Notice how speech patterns become visible as horizontal bands
:::
:::
:::
:::
:::

## The audio processing pipeline
### From sound waves to predictions

:::{style="margin-top: 30px; font-size: 22px;"}
:::{.columns}
:::{.column width=100%}
```{mermaid}
%%{init: {'theme': 'base', 'themeVariables': {'fontSize': '16px'}}}%%
flowchart LR
    A[🎤 Raw Audio] --> B[✂️ Slice into<br>windows]
    B --> C[📊 FFT<br>Fourier Transform]
    C --> D[🎵 Mel Scale<br>Mapping]
    D --> E[🖼️ 2D Mel<br>Spectrogram]
    E --> F[🧠 CNN or<br>Transformer]
    F --> G[📝 Output:<br>Text/Class/etc.]
    style E fill:#90EE90,stroke:#333,stroke-width:2px
    style F fill:#87CEEB,stroke:#333,stroke-width:2px
```

:::{style="margin-top: 30px;"}
1. **Slice**: Break audio into short windows (typically 25ms)
2. **FFT**: Convert each window from time domain to frequency domain
3. **Mel mapping**: Apply mel scale to match human perception
4. **Stack**: Create 2D image from all windows
5. **Process**: Use CNN or Transformer—[same as images!]{.alert}
:::
:::
:::
:::

## Whisper: Speech recognition
### OpenAI's multilingual marvel

:::{style="margin-top: 30px; font-size: 24px;"}
:::{.columns}
:::{.column width=55%}
- [Whisper]{.alert} (2022): OpenAI's speech-to-text model
- Trained on [680,000 hours]{.alert} of audio from the web
- Capabilities:
  - Speech recognition in [99 languages]{.alert}
  - Translation to English
  - Timestamps and speaker detection
- Architecture: [Encoder-decoder Transformer]{.alert}
  - Encoder: Processes mel spectrogram
  - Decoder: Generates text tokens
- Open source and free to use!
:::

:::{.column width=45%}
:::{style="text-align: center;"}
[![Whisper architecture](figures/whisper-architecture.png){width="100%"}](#){data-modal-type="image" data-modal-url="figures/whisper-architecture.png"}

Source: [OpenAI Whisper](https://openai.com/research/whisper)
:::
:::
:::
:::

## Voice cloning and music generation
### The creative (and concerning) frontier

:::{style="margin-top: 30px; font-size: 22px;"}
:::{.columns}
:::{.column width=55%}
**Voice Cloning:**

- [ElevenLabs]{.alert}: Clone any voice with minutes of audio
- Used for: Dubbing, audiobooks, accessibility
- Concerns: [Deepfake audio]{.alert}, fraud, impersonation

**Music Generation:**

- [Suno]{.alert}: Text-to-music ("upbeat jazz song about coding")
- [MusicLM]{.alert} (Google): High-quality music from descriptions
- [Udio]{.alert}: Another popular music generator

**The technology:**

- Autoregressive models (like LLMs, but for audio)
- Diffusion models (like image generators)
- Often combine both approaches
:::

:::{.column width=45%}
:::{style="text-align: center;"}
[![Voice cloning and music generation tools](figures/audio-generation.png){width="100%"}](#){data-modal-type="image" data-modal-url="figures/audio-generation.png"}

:::{style="font-size: 18px; margin-top: 15px;"}
**Try them:**

# Multimodal LLMs 🌐 {background-color="#2d4563"}

## The big picture
### All roads lead to embeddings!

:::{style="margin-top: 30px; font-size: 24px;"}
:::{.columns}
:::{.column width=55%}
- Here's the [key insight]{.alert} of this lecture:
- Whether it's text, images, or audio...
- Everything gets converted to [embeddings]{.alert}!
- [Same mathematical representation]{.alert}:
  - Text token → 4096-dimensional vector
  - Image patch → 4096-dimensional vector
  - Audio segment → 4096-dimensional vector
- Once in embedding space, the [LLM doesn't know the original modality]{.alert}!
- This enables [true multimodal understanding]{.alert}
:::

:::{.column width=45%}
:::{style="text-align: center;"}
[![All modalities converge to embeddings](figures/modality-embeddings.png){width="100%"}](#){data-modal-type="image" data-modal-url="figures/modality-embeddings.png"}

Source: [ByteByteGo](https://blog.bytebytego.com/)
:::
:::
:::
:::

## The three-part architecture
### How multimodal LLMs work

:::{style="margin-top: 30px; font-size: 22px;"}
:::{.columns}
:::{.column width=100%}
:::{style="text-align: center;"}
[![Multimodal LLM architecture: Encoder → Projector → LLM](figures/multimodal-llm-architecture.png){width="85%"}](#){data-modal-type="image" data-modal-url="figures/multimodal-llm-architecture.png"}
:::

:::{style="margin-top: 20px;"}
1. **Modality Encoder**: Vision Transformer (images) or Whisper (audio) — [pre-trained specialists]{.alert}
2. **Projection Layer**: Aligns encoder outputs to LLM's embedding space — [often surprisingly simple!]{.alert}
3. **LLM Backbone**: The "brain" (GPT-4, LLaMA, Claude) — processes everything as tokens
:::
:::
:::
:::

## How GPT-4V, Gemini, and Claude see
### Real-world multimodal models

:::{style="margin-top: 30px; font-size: 22px;"}
:::{.columns}
:::{.column width=55%}
**GPT-4V / GPT-4o (OpenAI):**

- Vision encoder + GPT-4
- Can analyse images, charts, documents, handwriting
- Powers ChatGPT's image understanding

**Gemini (Google):**

- Natively multimodal (trained on all modalities together)
- Handles text, images, audio, video
- Integrated into Google products

**Claude 3 (Anthropic):**

- Vision capabilities added in 2024
- Strong at document analysis and reasoning
- [All use similar underlying principles!]{.alert}
:::

:::{.column width=45%}
:::{style="text-align: center;"}
[![Comparison of multimodal LLMs](figures/multimodal-comparison.png){width="100%"}](#){data-modal-type="image" data-modal-url="figures/multimodal-comparison.png"}

:::{style="font-size: 18px; margin-top: 15px;"}
Despite different architectures, all convert images to embeddings that the LLM can process
:::

:::
:::

## Two architectural approaches
### Unified embedding vs cross-attention

:::{style="margin-top: 30px; font-size: 22px;"}
:::{.columns}
:::{.column width=50%}
**Unified Embedding (Simpler):**

- Concatenate image tokens with text tokens
- Feed everything into standard LLM
- [Used by]{.alert}: LLaVA, Fuyu, Pixtral

```
[IMG][IMG][IMG]...[TEXT][TEXT][TEXT]
        ↓
    Standard LLM
        ↓
      Output
```

- Pros: Simple, flexible
- Cons: Uses context window for images
:::

:::{.column width=50%}
**Cross-Attention (More Efficient):**

- Image features connected via special attention layers
- Text and image processed separately, then combined
- [Used by]{.alert}: Flamingo, LLaMA 3.2 Vision

```
[IMG features] ←→ [TEXT tokens]
         ↘     ↙
    Cross-attention
           ↓
        Output
```

- Pros: More efficient for high-res images
- Cons: More complex architecture
:::
:::
:::

## Training multimodal models
### Two-stage learning

:::{style="margin-top: 30px; font-size: 24px;"}
:::{.columns}
:::{.column width=55%}
**Stage 1: Feature Alignment**

- [Freeze]{.alert} vision encoder and LLM
- Only train the projection layer
- Goal: Learn that "dog image" and "dog text" should be close
- Dataset: Millions of image-caption pairs

**Stage 2: Instruction Tuning**

- [Unfreeze]{.alert} the LLM (often with efficient methods like LoRA)
- Train on instruction-response datasets
- Goal: Learn to follow complex multimodal instructions
- Dataset: "Describe this image", "What's wrong with this chart?"
:::

:::{.column width=45%}
:::{style="text-align: center;"}
[![Two-stage training process](figures/multimodal-training.png){width="100%"}](#){data-modal-type="image" data-modal-url="figures/multimodal-training.png"}

Source: [Sebastian Raschka](https://magazine.sebastianraschka.com/)
:::

## Ethical considerations ⚠️
### The darker side of multimodal AI

:::{style="margin-top: 30px; font-size: 22px;"}
:::{.columns}
:::{.column width=55%}
**Deepfakes and Misinformation:**

- Voice cloning can impersonate anyone
- Image generation creates realistic fakes
- Video deepfakes increasingly convincing

**Bias in Vision Systems:**

- Facial recognition [less accurate for darker skin]{.alert}
- Training data reflects societal biases
- Deployment in sensitive contexts (policing, hiring)

**Privacy Concerns:**

- Models trained on scraped internet data
- Can recognise faces, locations, personal information
- Surveillance applications

[These tools are powerful—use them responsibly!]{.alert}
:::

:::{.column width=45%}
:::{style="text-align: center;"}
[![Ethical concerns with multimodal AI](figures/ai-ethics.png){width="100%"}](#){data-modal-type="image" data-modal-url="figures/ai-ethics.png"}

:::{style="font-size: 18px; margin-top: 15px;"}
Remember: Technology is neutral, but its applications aren't
:::

# Summary 📚 {background-color="#2d4563"}

## Main takeaways

:::{style="margin-top: 30px; font-size: 28px;"}

- `r fa('image')` Images are [grids of numbers]{.alert}; CNNs use convolution to detect features (edges → objects)

- `r fa('th')` [Vision Transformers]{.alert} treat images as patches—just like tokens in text!

- `r fa('tasks')` Computer vision tasks: [classification]{.alert} (what?), [detection]{.alert} (where?), [segmentation]{.alert} (which pixels?)

- `r fa('music')` Audio becomes [spectrograms]{.alert}—2D images that can be processed by the same models

- `r fa('brain')` [Multimodal LLMs]{.alert}: All modalities (text, image, audio) become embeddings in shared space

- `r fa('link')` Architecture: [Encoder → Projector → LLM]{.alert} — the projector bridges different modalities

- `r fa('exclamation-triangle')` [Ethical concerns]{.alert}: Deepfakes, bias in vision systems, privacy implications
:::
